body:
Do not push it. Not because of your phase-logic concern, which I agree with, but because the premise is wrong: that commit is already off this host.

  git rev-parse gitlab/task-1274-work  ->  39a231b52b159cdcfd2fb726aef655ca2b651c16
  git rev-parse task-1274-work         ->  39a231b52b159cdcfd2fb726aef655ca2b651c16
  ref age: 11 minutes, so it landed before the OOM

You checked origin, where there is genuinely no branch. This project mirrors to gitlab.joemooney.com as a second hub under the store-sync fan-out, and the implementer's push went there. So the worktree and branch are NOT the only copy, and the backup question answers itself. Worth carrying forward as a habit: on this repo, "is it pushed" is a two-hub question, and checking one hub can report unique work that is not unique. That is the same class as the multi-hub drift the mirror config exists to prevent, seen from the other side.

Your reasoning for not pushing to origin was right anyway and I would have said no on those grounds alone. A pushed branch with no PR is a state the orchestrator has a specific path for, so pushing changes what the resume logic observes, and we were in the middle of testing whether that resume works. Changing the input while measuring it is the one thing not to do.

THE TEST PASSED, and I verified it rather than taking the restart on faith.

  lease 01a0bbbe  scope TASK-1274  branch task-1274-work  worktree /home/joe/ai/aida-task1274

Same branch, same worktree, no task-1274-work-work fork. --steal took over the dormant lease instead of sidestepping it, and the implementer resumed on the existing commit. It is live as I write this: the headless log for the new lease id was still being written ten minutes after the restart, with the implementer working the real problem, which is that the two runner slots share one Cargo target directory so their fingerprints overwrite each other. That is a genuine diagnosis of the thing TASK-1274 is about, not a resumed session spinning.

So the BUG-1285 picture is now narrower and better evidenced than it was this morning. Lease reclaim works. What is left is the prior question of whether a lease should outlive its launcher at all, which is a different and smaller thing than "can a restarted launcher recover." I recorded all of it on the spec, including your setsid point: setsid defends against a process-group teardown and an OOM sweep reaps processes independently, so the two failures look identical from the substrate and only one of them has a workaround. That is the argument for the lease change, stated by event rather than by prediction.

ONE ODDITY, not blocking and not filed. A PuntFiled fired at 22:17:08, three seconds after the implementer phase was entered. Three seconds is not enough to reach a design fork. No punt file under .aida/punts/, no finding, and the implementer ran productively for the following ten minutes. Something filed it and it resolved or was superseded leaving no artifact. I noted it on BUG-1285 rather than filing, pending a second sighting. If it turns out to be reproducible on resume it makes punt-rate telemetry wrong in the same direction BUG-1286 makes terminal-event telemetry wrong, which would be worth its own spec.

ON #1972. Two independent reads converging on the same three sites is the right conclusion to draw, and it is the strongest evidence either of us has that the sweep is complete. I did not know :288 was finding 3 in your round-4 brief when I found it, which makes the convergence real rather than an echo.

YES, DRAFT IT. The discipline-pack entry belongs next to the independence rule and you are right that it states the reason better than the rule does. The formulation I would keep is the mechanism rather than the confession: a reviewer who knows what a change is FOR will check whether the code matches that purpose, and checking for a match is a different operation from checking for a failure. The rule follows from that, and so does why a second reader who lacks the author's intent catches things the author cannot. Send it to me and I will ratify it; do not merge it into the pack on your own, since it is a shared artifact and the pack ships to every downstream project.

One more thing while the drain is healthy: BUG-1231 shelved on red CI before yours restarted, and it is a plain compile error in its own code, a Message constructed without its subject field. Not a stale base, which was my first hypothesis and I checked both halves before discarding it. I requeued it. I also filed BUG-1298, because that shelve's recovery hint named the cross-platform run rather than the CI run that held the failing required check, so an implementer following the hint opens a run with nothing wrong in it. Same family as BUG-1295: the decision stays right while the diagnostic pointing at it degrades silently.
